strengths: Timely and novel direction: the paper is among the first to adapt a diffusion LLM (LLaDA-8B-Instruct) to offline black-box optimization, exploiting bidirectional modeling to address a genuine limitation of autoregressive LLM generators.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: four Design-Bench tasks spanning discrete (TF Bind 8/10) and continuous (Ant/D'Kitty) domains, 8 seeds, both 100th-percentile and median metrics, with DiBO achieving the best mean/median rank overall.

Systematic ablations and sensitivity analyses that isolate the contribution of delimiter tokens, each training stage (DA/SFT/RL), and similarity-conditioned context construction, plus hyperparameter studies (context length, pool size, RL learning rate, prompt templates).

Practical, reproducible engineering design: a unified prompt-response corpus, explicit delimiter tokens, and reported hyperparameters (learning rates, optimizer, batch sizes, hardware), with prompt templates and data-construction details in the appendix.
Honest reporting of a case where the method underperforms (D'Kitty) and inclusion of a limitations/impact statement.
weaknesses: The central motivation—that bidirectional modeling is the source of gains—is never isolated. There is no controlled comparison against an autoregressive LLM fine-tuned with the identical DA+SFT+RL pipeline. The only AR baseline (OPRO) is prompt-only, so improvements could plausibly stem from domain adaptation/post-training rather than bidirectionality, leaving the paper's core claim unverified.

The RL objective (Eq. 7) is non-standard and under-justified: it weights the loss by the probability p_θ(o_k) rather than log p_θ(o_k) (inconsistent with the log-prob approximation in Eq. 6), and omits clipping, KL regularization, and reward centering. The justification ('old policy assumed uniform') is weak; as written this may be a typo or a poorly-motivated objective, which is a material soundness concern for the RL stage.

The method's strong performance depends heavily on the similarity-conditioned context construction (TF Bind 8 drops from 0.965 to 0.730 when random context is used). This suggests the model is largely performing local refinement of a near-neighbor design already present in the pool rather than genuine global generative optimization, which undercuts the paper's 'robust generalization' narrative and is neither analyzed nor bounded.

Baseline fairness and tuning are unclear. Several baselines were designed for the full Design-Bench datasets, and the paper does not describe how they were tuned for the 500-sample regime, so part of the reported margin may reflect suboptimal baseline configuration. The most closely related prior work (dLLM+MCTS, Yuan et al. 2026) is deliberately excluded from the main comparison, so the 'state-of-the-art' claim is not established against the nearest competitor.
The one-step unmasking approximation for log-probability (Eq. 6) is not justified or validated against iterative denoising, and its effect on the RL signal is unknown.

Some results show suspiciously low variance (e.g., D'Kitty 0.923 ± 0.002) alongside large margins, yet no statistical significance testing is provided; the primary metric (max over 128 candidates) is inherently high-variance and can reward extreme sampling rather than reliable optimization.

Missing reproducibility details: size and construction of the RL reward dataset, the balancing procedure for positive/negative rewards, and baseline hyperparameters are not fully specified; the code link is removed in the submission.

strengths: Timely and interesting direction: applying diffusion LLMs (LLaDA-8B) to offline BBO to exploit bidirectional context, which is a genuinely underexplored angle relative to the dominant AR-LLM prompting line of work.

Reasonable, well-motivated engineering: a unified prompt-response corpus with explicit delimiter tokens, and a similarity-conditioned context construction that the ablation (Table 4) shows is highly consequential (TF8: 0.730 -> 0.965).

Strong headline results on the standard benchmark for several tasks, most notably TF Bind 8 (0.965 ± 0.038 vs. best baseline MCTS-transfer 0.857) and competitive Ant results, with 8-seed mean/std and rank-based aggregation.

The ablation suite is fairly thorough: delimiter tokens across all stages (Table 2), stage removal (Table 3), and hyperparameter sensitivity (context length, pool size, LR, prompt templates, Fig. 2), which supports the individual components.
Reproducibility-friendly setup details (single H100, ~1.5h per task, listed learning rates, bnb optimizer, masking schedule from the official implementation).
weaknesses: The central scientific claim—that diffusion LLMs' *bidirectional modeling* is what drives the gains—is not validated. The only AR comparison is OPRO (prompting-only with LLaMA3-8B), so the improvement could come entirely from the DA+SFT+RL training pipeline rather than from bidirectional modeling. A controlled experiment running the identical pipeline with an AR backbone is needed to support the main motivation.

The RL objective as written (Eq. 7) is inconsistent with the log-probability approximation it claims to use (Eq. 6) and with standard policy-gradient/REINFORCE: it uses p_θ(o_k|...) rather than log p_θ(o_k|...) inside the expectation. This is either an error or an unjustified design choice; as stated it is not the reward-weighted likelihood the text implies.

The decision to omit reward centering 'to preserve the inherent prompt-specific information' (Sec. 3.2) is questionable and runs counter to standard variance-reduction practice for offline RL; no justification or empirical support is given for this deviation.

The one-step, fully-masked approximation log p_θ(o|q) ≈ Σ_k log p_θ(o_k | q, o_fullmask) ignores inter-token dependencies during denoising and may be a poor surrogate for the actual diffusion generation probability; this is not analyzed.

The 'state-of-the-art' claim is carried mainly by TF Bind 8. On D'Kitty Morphology DiBO (0.923) is beaten by ExPT (0.950) and several others, and on Ant Morphology the gap to ExPT (0.944 vs. 0.929) is within one std; the rank-aggregation framing masks this task-level heterogeneity.

A methodological confound: responses are chosen to be high-label *and* similar to the prompt context, so the method may largely perform retrieval/local search around near-optimal labeled samples. The paper does not disentangle genuine 'optimization' from nearest-neighbor-like copying of high-label designs.

Presentation and bibliography are sloppy in ways that undermine confidence: garbled years (Grattafori et al. '2006', Hansen '2018', Raffel et al. '2025', Novikov '2020' vs. text '2025'), duplicate references (Nie et al. 2024 twice; Yuan et al. 2023a/2023b), and the use of 'GPT-5.2' to generate prompt templates, which is unverifiable and suspicious.

Reproducibility gaps: the code link is given only as 'here', and key details—how 60/56-dim continuous designs are tokenized/serialized, how candidate designs are decoded and de-duplicated at inference, and the exact RL sampling—are missing or relegated to an appendix that is thin on these points.

Scope is narrow: only Design-Bench, very short discrete sequences (length 8-10), a single 8B backbone, and no discussion of compute/latency costs relative to the strong forward baselines it claims to beat.

strengths: The paper makes a useful and original contribution by adapting diffusion LLMs to offline BBO, leveraging bidirectional modeling that is well motivated for design problems with non-sequential dependencies such as DNA sequences.

The unified prompt-response corpus with explicit delimiter tokens is a sensible and empirically effective solution to the domain gap; Table 2 shows consistent gains across DA, SFT, and RL stages, with a large DA gain on Ant (0.693 -> 0.875).
The three-stage pipeline (DA, SFT, RL) is systematically ablated in Table 3; all stages contribute, and the failure of RL-only on Ant is a useful diagnostic about the necessity of prior alignment.

The empirical results are strong on Design-Bench small-data: DiBO achieves the best mean score (0.897) and best mean/median rank (2.5/1.0) in Table 1, and is state-of-the-art on Ant, TF8, and TF10, with a large margin on TF8 (0.965 vs. 0.857).
Median results in Appendix A.4 also show DiBO with the best mean score (0.621) and median rank 1.5, supporting robustness beyond best-of-128 evaluation.

The similarity-conditioned context construction is a valuable finding: Table 4 shows a large gain over random context (0.965 vs. 0.730 on TF8), highlighting the importance of local semantic consistency for diffusion-LLM optimization.
Hyperparameter sensitivity in Figure 2 shows robustness to RL learning rate and prompt template variation, and reasonable trends with context length and offline dataset size.
Implementation details, prompt templates, and training hyperparameters are largely provided; training is feasible on a single H100 (e.g., 1.5 h for TF8), which aids reproducibility.
The impact statement acknowledges risks of misuse and bias and calls for responsible deployment, which is appropriate for a generative optimization method.
weaknesses: The RL objective as written appears inconsistent: Eq. 6 approximates log p(o|q) with a sum of log probabilities, but Eq. 7 uses p_theta(o_k | q, o_fullmask) without the log. If literal, this is not a standard policy-gradient/REINFORCE objective and may not optimize the intended log-likelihood. This needs correction or clarification.

The domain adaptation loss in Eq. 3 is ambiguous or malformed: the indicator is only on o_t^i = [M], yet the log term predicts q_0^i and o_0^i jointly conditioned on q_t, o_t, and the text says both prompt and response are reconstructed. The masking scheme and loss definition should be made precise.

The closest prior work, inference-only diffusion LLM + MCTS (Yuan et al., 2026), is listed as a baseline but not quantitatively compared in the main tables; it is only discussed in Appendix A.5. A direct comparison under matched conditions, or at least inclusion with caveats, is important for state-of-the-art claims.

Evaluation is limited to four Design-Bench tasks. Despite broad claims about robotics, DNA, and materials discovery, no additional real-world or scientific design domains are tested, so generalization remains unclear.

There is no explicit Limitations section; only scattered constraints are noted, such as GPU memory and context length. Failure modes such as D'Kitty underperformance versus ExPT/COMs and the RL-only formatting failure deserve more discussion.

The one-step unmasking approximation used for RL creates a train-inference mismatch: training approximates log p with a single unmasking step, while inference uses iterative denoising. No analysis is provided on how well this approximation tracks full denoising.

The RL reward design omits reward centering without ablation, and the construction and balancing of positive and negative rewards in D_rl are not fully specified, making the RL signal hard to assess and reproduce.
Reference and citation errors (e.g., Dettmers et al. 2006 vs. 2022; Grattafori et al. 2006 vs. 2024; Le et al. 2020 vs. 2018) and an apparently missing code link reduce polish and reproducibility.

No statistical significance tests are reported. Improvements on some tasks (e.g., TF10: 0.755 vs. 0.730) may be within noise given the reported standard deviations, and the paper relies heavily on rank aggregation for its main claim.

strengths: The core idea of adapting diffusion LLMs to offline black-box optimization is novel and well-motivated, exploiting bidirectional (non-causal) modeling that is plausibly better suited to design problems with non-sequential dependencies (e.g., DNA).

The matched diffusion-vs-autoregressive comparison (Table 2) is a genuinely informative controlled experiment: it holds the prompt construction, delimiter tokens, data, context selection, and the full DA→SFT→RL pipeline fixed while swapping only the backbone, and shows consistent gains for the diffusion backbone. This is the strongest evidence for the paper's central hypothesis.

The ablation suite is reasonably thorough: delimiter tokens (Table 3), removal of each training stage (Table 4), similarity-conditioned context (Table 5), pool sub-sampling strategy (Table 6), and hyperparameter sensitivity (Figure 2) collectively isolate the contribution of each component.

The pretraining-overlap audit (Appendix A.7) is a thoughtful and unusual piece of diligence that probes whether the frozen LLMADA checkpoint already encodes benchmark-specific design-label knowledge; the near-random ranking results make a reasonable case against leakage.
The paper includes an impact statement acknowledging bias amplification and misuse risks in biochemical contexts, and treats the ethics of the domain appropriately.

Reproducibility details (learning rates, batch sizes, accumulation steps, number of optimization steps, optimizer, hardware, and per-task training time) are reported in enough detail to be actionable.
weaknesses: The headline 'state-of-the-art on Design-Bench' claim rests on an unfair comparison: DiBO is an 8B-parameter model initialized from a large pretrained LLM (LLaDA-8B-Instruct), whereas most baselines (COMs, CbAS, MIN, BONET, DDOM, GTG, etc.) are task-specific models trained from scratch on the same 500 samples. The advantage may largely reflect pretrained scale/prior rather than the proposed diffusion-BBO methodology, and no compute- or parameter-matched comparison against a from-scratch baseline is provided. The authors' own matched AR comparison partly addresses this for the diffusion claim but not for the SOTA claim against the broader baseline set.

The reinforcement-learning objective is technically questionable and internally inconsistent. Equation 6 explicitly approximates log p(o|q) via a sum of log-probabilities, yet Equation 7 uses p_θ (not log p_θ) inside the loss. It is unclear whether this is a typo or intentional; if intentional, the resulting objective is a non-standard reward-weighted probability maximization with different gradient weighting and vanishing-gradient behavior, which is not clearly a valid policy-gradient surrogate. Additionally, dropping importance-sampling ratios, clipping, KL regularization, and reward centering (the 'advantage' is r/σ with no baseline) is a strong simplification justified only by assuming a uniform behavior policy; the stated rationale ('preserving prompt-specific information') is weak, and the omission of centering typically inflates variance.

The relevance of the RL stage is not strongly established. In Table 4, removing RL from the full pipeline (DA+SFT) costs only 0.014 (TF8) and 0.009 (Ant), while the paper frames RL as a central contribution. The ablation evidence does not clearly justify the added complexity and the questionable objective.
Reproducibility is undercut by a broken/placeholder code link ('Code for our work is available here' with no URL), despite the abstract promising released code.

The reference list shows signs of citation padding and contains many unrelated or implausible entries (e.g., a 3D point-cloud completion paper, a retrieval-augmented LLM personalization/bandits paper, a 4D point-cloud paper) that have no bearing on offline BBO, as well as many 2026-dated citations. This raises concerns about scholarly rigor and, at minimum, distracts from and weakens the related-work framing.

The evaluation is limited to four Design-Bench tasks (with the two continuous tasks showing small or negative margins: DiBO underperforms ExPT on D'Kitty by 0.027 at the 100th percentile), and the paper itself notes the RNA results are 'mixed.' The single strongest result (TF Bind 8) plus near-ties elsewhere does not robustly support a broad SOTA claim.

The paper excludes the most directly comparable prior work (Yuan et al., 2026, diffusion LLMs for BBO) from the main comparison, arguing it targets an extremely few-shot regime (n_pool=10). A head-to-head comparison under the authors' own n_pool=500 setting would materially strengthen or refute the claimed advantage of training over inference-only diffusion prompting.

The 'small-data' regime (n_pool=500) is constructed by sub-sampling the full Design-Bench datasets rather than following the standard fixed offline splits, which complicates direct comparison to previously published numbers and should be more carefully justified as a valid benchmark variant.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and reasonable problem: adapting diffusion (masked) LLMs to offline black-box optimization, which is a genuinely underexplored direction relative to the many AR-LLM-for-BBO works.

The pipeline is coherent and well-organized: a unified prompt-response corpus with explicit delimiter tokens (Section 3.1), followed by DA -> SFT -> RL post-training (Section 3.2). The design is easy to follow.

The empirical study is broad: four Design-Bench tasks, 15+ baselines, matched diffusion-vs-AR comparison (Table 2), component ablations (Tables 3-6), hyperparameter sensitivity (Figure 2), plus Top-K and RNA results in the appendix.
The pretraining-overlap audit via ranking probing (Appendix A.7) is a thoughtful and honest attempt to address a real contamination concern for LLM-based BBO.
Reproducibility is documented reasonably well: base model (LLaDA-8B-Instruct), learning rates, batch sizes, steps, hardware (single H100), and reported wall-clock (~1.5h for TF8).
The authors are candid about D'Kitty underperformance and the mixed RNA results, which is a positive signal.
weaknesses: The reinforcement-learning formulation appears technically inconsistent. Equation 6 explicitly defines an approximation to log p(o|q) and states it is 'required by the RL objective,' yet Equation 7 uses p(o_k|q, o_fullmask) directly, not log p. As written, the objective is reward-weighted behavior cloning (maximize p*r for positive r, minimize for negative r), not policy-gradient RL, and the 'assume the old policy is uniform' argument is used to discard importance sampling, clipping, and KL regularization entirely. The RL stage is therefore mislabeled and underspecified, and its marginal contribution is small anyway (Table 4: +0.014 on TF8, +0.032 on Ant over DA+SFT).

The headline results appear to be driven mainly by the similarity-conditioned context construction rather than by diffusion modeling. Table 5 shows that removing the locality constraint collapses TF8 from 0.965 to 0.730 (a 0.235 drop), far larger than any diffusion-vs-AR or delimiter effect. This raises a leakage/realism concern: because responses are selected to be near-neighbors of the prompt context, the task reduces to local improvement, and it is unclear how context is selected at inference time ('independently resample the corresponding context examples from the offline pool') — if random at test time, there is a serious train/test mismatch.

Fairness of the baseline comparison is unclear. The paper claims a 'small-data setting' with n_pool=500, and Appendix A.1 states the same pool is used for all comparison methods, yet the reported baseline numbers closely resemble published full-dataset Design-Bench results. The paper does not clearly state whether baselines were retrained on the 500-sample pool or copied from the literature, which is decisive for interpreting Table 1.

Support for the central 'bidirectional modeling' hypothesis is weak. In the matched comparison (Table 2), the diffusion advantage at the final RL stage is 0.050 (TF8), 0.073 (TF10), 0.011 (Ant) and 0.001 (D'Kitty); the continuous-task gains are essentially within noise. This is confounded by the different pretraining corpora of LLaDA-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B, so the comparison does not isolate causality.

The single most relevant prior work — dLLM (Yuan et al., 2026), which also applies diffusion LLMs to BBO — is excluded from the main comparison on the grounds that it targets n_pool=10. Excluding the closest competitor without a direct comparison (even under matched conditions) weakens the claim of state-of-the-art.

Several claims are overstated. Delimiter tokens are described as 'critical,' yet on TF8 the difference is only 0.022 (0.943 vs 0.965), which is within roughly half a standard deviation; the 'critical' framing is only justified by the single Ant DA point.

Evaluation emphasizes the 100th-percentile (best of 128) score as the main metric, which is a weak and high-variance indicator; the more informative median results are relegated to the appendix and show smaller margins.

Presentation problems reduce confidence: typos and inconsistencies in the tables (e.g., 'D(best)'/'T(best)', 'UniSO-T' vs 'UniSOT'), and the RL objective equations are hard to reconcile with the surrounding text.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: offline black-box optimization in small-data regimes, and proposes adapting diffusion LLMs to exploit bidirectional modeling.
The unified prompt-response corpus with explicit delimiter tokens for designs and labels is a simple, intuitive way to bridge heterogeneous BBO signals and natural-language pretraining.
The three-stage pipeline (domain adaptation, SFT, RL) is clearly motivated and supported by an ablation showing that all stages contribute (Table 4).
The matched diffusion-vs-autoregressive comparison (Table 2) provides direct evidence that the bidirectional diffusion backbone outperforms a comparable AR backbone across tasks and stages.
Empirical results on four Design-Bench tasks with 8 seeds, plus top-K and median metrics in the appendix, are extensive; DiBO achieves strong 100th-percentile scores on Ant, TF8, and TF10.
The pretraining-overlap audit in Appendix A.7 is a thoughtful attempt to rule out benchmark leakage from the pretrained diffusion LLM.
The paper includes hyperparameter sensitivity analyses, prompt-template variation, and additional RNA tasks, which improve confidence in robustness.
weaknesses: The central claim of state-of-the-art performance under small-data settings is not convincingly supported. The baseline numbers in Table 1 appear to match standard full-data Design-Bench results (e.g., ExPT Ant 0.929, D'Kitty 0.950, TF8 0.810, TF10 0.703; COMs and Grad-mean also match known full-data results), yet the paper states that all methods use the same n_pool=500 pool. It is not described how baselines were retrained or adapted to the small-data regime, so the comparison is likely not apples-to-apples.

The RL objective in Eq. 7 is inconsistent with the stated log-probability approximation. Eq. 6 defines log p(o|q) approximately as sum_k log p(o_k | q, o_fullmask), but Eq. 7 uses p_theta(o_k | ...) without the log. A reward-weighted sum of probabilities is not the standard policy-gradient objective and lacks justification; if it is a typo, the central RL equation is still incorrectly presented.

The assumption that the behavior policy is uniform is strong and unrealistic for offline BBO datasets collected from real design processes. Dropping importance-ratio clipping and KL regularization is not well justified, and the theoretical basis for the RL stage is weak.

Reproducibility is limited: the code availability statement says code is available 'here' but no URL is visible in the manuscript; details such as initialization of new delimiter-token embeddings, exact RL dataset construction, and baseline training under n_pool=500 are not fully specified.
Several references appear incorrect or future-dated (e.g., arXiv:2605.11246, arXiv:2601.14446, arXiv:2602.18735, and 'ChatGPT-5.2'), which raises concerns about citation accuracy and scholarship.

The additional RNA experiments in Appendix A.6 are mixed: DiBO is worse than baselines on many Top-K and median metrics and on RNA-B entirely, which tempers the claimed robustness and generality of the method.

The main text overstates consistency across domains by focusing on 100th-percentile Design-Bench results while the appendix shows weaker performance on other metrics and tasks. The limitations of the method are not discussed in a dedicated limitations section.

The RL-only variant fails on Ant Morphology, and the full pipeline's gains over SFT+RL are modest (e.g., TF8 0.965 vs. 0.951; Ant 0.945 vs. 0.913), suggesting the RL contribution may be limited relative to SFT.

The context length is capped at 7 few-shot examples due to GPU memory, and no results are shown beyond that; the method requires an 8B diffusion LLM and an H100, which limits accessibility and practical reproducibility.
